catalog_quote: SYLLABLE STRESS Stress (or emphasis or accent) typically falls on syllable or syllables marked with special symbols (e.g., wétu stresses first syllable with primary/main stress; ewò stresses second with a low/falling tone; wuskówhàn has main stress & low pitch; aúï stresses aú and ï). Narragansett is well-stressed, although inconsistently and ambiguously (G. Aubin, 1972). Most Massachusett language words in Eliot seem to have no stress marks. This may indicate either that no special stress on any one syllable exists [e.g., nippe, ask∞k, mehtugq], or it was omitted intentionally for fluent speakers of the language being taught the Bible in their own oral language. new_statements.quote: Accent structure for Narragansett-Massachusett has not been fully worked out in the theoretical linguistics literature. [...] Algonquianist Professor G. Aubin, a respected correspondent of the Aquidneck Indian Council, relates in a personal e-mail communication of 6-25-2002, the possible applicability of the following efficient “Ojibway-like rule” for long/short vowels (cf. Goddard and Bragdon, 1988): o All long vowels are stressed o All alternate even-numbered short vowels are stressed This rules presupposes the existence of correct vowel classification which has not been achieved for the extinct American Indian languages Massachusett-Narragansett.
new_statements.citation: O'Brien, Frank Waabu (Francis J. O'Brien Jr.). 2005. American Indian Studies in the Extinct Languages of Southeastern New England. Newport, RI: Aquidneck Indian Council (ERIC ED490469).

Aubin, a respected correspondent of the Aquidneck Indian Council, relates in a personal e-mail communication of 6-25-2002, the possible applicability of the following efficient \"Ojibway-like rule\" for long/short vowels (cf. Goddard and Bragdon, 1988): o All long vowels are…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tentative, second-hand (Aubin p.c. reported by O'Brien): a quantity-sensitive rhythmic pattern of the general Eastern Algonquian/Ojibwe type — every long vowel bears stress, and among short-vowel syllables every second (even-numbered) one is stressed; O'Brien adds (p.240) that in practice stress is read off Williams' 1643 accent marks (á, à, â), which Aubin 1972 judged inconsistent, so placement is treated as largely unknown.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None stated as such; the alternating-count clause implies rhythmic secondary stresses. O'Brien's chart glosses à as 'secondary stress' but says historic records 'seem to omit' it.
new_statements.exceptions: Author stresses the rule 'presupposes... correct vowel classification which has not been achieved'; 'Narragansett is well-stressed, although inconsistently and ambiguously (G. Aubin, 1972)'; Massachusett words in Eliot mostly carry no stress marks.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent as marked on citation forms in Roger Williams' 1643 Narragansett vocabulary/phrases; statement is framed for 'Narragansett-Massachusett' jointly, not for Mohegan-Pequot proper.
new_statements.identity_note: The only rule-like statement found concerns Narragansett (Roger Williams' 1643 dialect; Glottolog narr1280, ISO xnt, which Glottolog files as a dialect under mohe1244) and is given jointly for 'Narragansett-Massachusett' (Massachusett = wamp1249, a different Glottolog language). For Mohegan-Pequot proper (Fidelia Fielding's dialect, d. 1908; the basis of the modern Fielding/Costa standard) no source opened states where stress falls: Speck 1928 only says stress is marked with an acute in his transcriptions, Prince & Speck 1903 note Mrs Fielding's own spelling marks no stress, and S. Fielding's 2006/2012 dictionary-grammar gives no stress rule (one entry, nuqut 'one', is annotated 'accent falls on 2nd syllable'). Granberry 2003 describes 'the dialect of Jits Bodunaxa' (= Fidelia Fielding) but could not be opened.

Aubin, 1972)'; reports Aubin p.c. 2002 'Ojibway-like rule': all long vowels stressed, alternate even-numbered short vowels stressed (cf. Goddard & Bragdon 1988). Second-hand, revivalist compilation.

sources.citation: Williams, Roger. 1643. A Key into the Language of America. London: Gregory Dexter (read in scanned of two 1643 copies, the 1827 Providence reprint, and Trumbull's 1866 Narragansett Club edition).

sources.note: 'Directions for the use of the Language' para 5: author affixed 'Accents, Tones or sounds' (acutes, graves, circumflexes) to each word and instructs that 'the sound or Tone' be put on the marked syllable (Ewò on wò; Ascowequássin on quáss; Anspaumpmaûntam on maûn, 'the Circumflex or long sounding Accent'). Accent recorded per word; no rule. Trumbull 1866 preface p.16: accents 'scrupulously retained'.

sources.note: Pronunciation Guide (pp.2-3) treats consonants, vowels, digraphs only; no word-stress rule anywhere in 220 pp. One dictionary entry: 'nuqut, NUM one (accent falls on 2nd syllable)'. Orthography phonemicized with David Costa's help (Guide).

sources.note: No stress statement; 'Abenaki Syncope' of short vowels is optional in oldest Pequot records but 'virtually obligatory in modern Mohegan', conditioning 'seems to depend on currently ill-understood metrical factors (Ives Goddard p.c.)' (pp.96-99, fn.72).

sources.citation: Goddard, Ives. 1981. Massachusett Phonology: A Preliminary Look. Papers of the Twelfth Algonquian Conference, 57-105. Ottawa: Carleton University.
sources.note: About Massachusett (wamp1249) but with remarks on our varieties: Williams' Narragansett accent 'most likely indicating stress' on reflexes of PA *i after an initial short-vowel syllable (p.74-75); 'Speck's recordings of Mohegan consistently indicate a stressed long vowel before the /y/' in II colour verbs (§14); unstressed Mass. /a/ 'as determined by a rhythmic stress pattern similar to that of other Algonquian languages' (§29). No rule for Mohegan-Pequot/Narragansett.
